world.dek: The Vesuvius Challenge, a US-backed competition offering millions in prize money, helped researchers recover the full text of a Herculaneum scroll without unrolling it.
world.heroCaption: A carbonized papyrus scroll from Herculaneum, buried by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 CE and now readable for the first time with AI.

body.text: For nearly two thousand years, a library's worth of scrolls sat sealed inside a villa in Herculaneum, carbonized into fragile black lumps by the same volcanic eruption that buried Pompeii in 79 CE. Any attempt to physically unroll them destroys them instantly, which is exactly why they'd never been read, until researchers this year managed to recover the complete text of one scroll using artificial intelligence, without ever touching the ancient papyrus itself.

The breakthrough is the latest milestone from the Vesuvius Challenge, a competition founded by US technology executives that has now paid out $1.8 million in prize money to researchers and computer scientists racing to crack open these ancient documents virtually. The approach combines high-resolution CT scanning with machine learning models trained to detect the faint traces of carbon-based ink on carbonized papyrus, then digitally unrolls the scroll's internal layers into a flat, readable surface.
How You Read a Scroll You Can Never Open

The technical challenge here is genuinely strange, even by archaeology standards. The scrolls are scanned inside a particle accelerator to produce extraordinarily detailed 3D X-ray images, since standard imaging can't distinguish carbon-based ink from the carbonized papyrus it sits on, the two are nearly identical in density. Machine learning models trained on thousands of scanned fragments learn to pick out the subtle textural differences that mark where ink was applied, effectively teaching a computer to see something the human eye simply cannot.

Nat Friedman, the US tech executive who helped found and fund the Vesuvius Challenge, described this latest full-scroll result as only the beginning, and said researchers expect meaningful further improvements in both the AI algorithms and the ink-detection methods that made the breakthrough possible. He's also been actively recruiting more computing talent to join the effort, betting that the hardest technical problems left in the project are exactly the kind that a wider pool of researchers might crack faster.
A Broader Wave of AI Meeting Ancient History

The Herculaneum breakthrough isn't happening in isolation. Across American universities, classics and digital humanities departments have quietly become some of the more surprising adopters of cutting-edge AI over the past couple of years. At the University of Iowa, classics professor Paul Dilley recently secured a $500,000 grant from the philanthropic research funder Schmidt Sciences to train AI models capable of suggesting plausible reconstructions for missing or damaged sections of ancient manuscripts, a project he expects to run for the next three years.

Dilley has been careful to frame the technology as a research aid rather than a replacement for traditional scholarship, emphasizing that human experts still need to have the final word on what a damaged passage most likely said. Similar caution runs through much of the field. Researchers at the University of Notre Dame have spent recent years developing neural networks capable of transcribing complex medieval handwriting, and have already adapted the system to read Ethiopian manuscripts written in an entirely different character set, a first step toward tools that could eventually handle multiple ancient languages at once.
The Limits of What AI Can Actually Do Here

Not every part of this pipeline is going smoothly. A recent benchmarking study testing large language models against the full workflow of preparing a scholarly digital edition found that while top AI systems scored above 90 out of 100 on straightforward ancient-language translation and grammar parsing, their performance dropped sharply, down to 60 to 74 out of 100, when asked to generate the structured technical metadata scholars actually need to catalog a manuscript properly. The models frequently invented catalog formats that don't exist or misapplied technical markup, a reminder that reading ancient text and correctly documenting it for other researchers remain two very different problems.

Rutgers digital humanities librarian Francesca Giannetti, who has watched the field evolve closely, says classicists arrived at a similar realization early on: computational tools would clearly help with the grinding, technical work of the discipline, but they were never going to substitute for the trained judgment scholars bring to interpreting what a damaged or ambiguous passage actually means. The Herculaneum scroll result suggests just how far the technical side of that partnership has already come, even as the harder questions of meaning and context remain firmly in human hands.

world.headline: NVIDIA and Nokia Partner on AI-Native 6G, T-Mobile Trials Begin
world.dek: The partnership pairs NVIDIA's telecom computing chips with Nokia's radio equipment, betting AI built into wireless networks is the key to America's next-gen mobile race.
world.heroCaption: Engineers test AI-RAN equipment at an NVIDIA and Nokia demonstration site, part of the companies' push toward AI-native 6G networks.

body.text: NVIDIA and Nokia are betting that the fight over 6G won't be won on raw data speeds alone, it'll be won on which networks can think for themselves. The two companies announced a strategic partnership this month to build commercial-grade AI-RAN products, essentially wireless network hardware with artificial intelligence baked directly into the radio access layer, on top of NVIDIA's computing platforms. T-Mobile has signed on as an early collaborator, with field trials expected to begin later this year focused on validating real-world performance and efficiency gains.

At the center of the announcement is a new piece of hardware NVIDIA is calling the Arc Aerial RAN Computer, a telecom computing platform the company describes as 6G-ready. Nokia plans to fold NVIDIA-powered, AI-RAN products into its existing radio access network portfolio, while Dell Technologies is contributing PowerEdge servers to help power the resulting systems. It's a genuinely unusual lineup, chipmaker, telecom equipment vendor, server maker, and wireless carrier all working from the same architecture at once.
Why AI Inside the Network, Not Just On Top of It

The pitch behind AI-RAN is straightforward, even if the engineering underneath it is not: today's cellular networks run on radio access algorithms that are, in NVIDIA's own description, roughly fifty years old at their core. Threading AI directly into that layer, rather than treating it as an add-on service running elsewhere, is supposed to squeeze meaningfully more spectral efficiency out of the same physical airwaves, while also giving networks the horsepower to handle a coming wave of AI-heavy traffic, from generative AI assistants on phones to autonomous drones and robots that will need near-instant, reliable connections.

NVIDIA's telecom lead, Ronnie Vasishta, has described this as building the intelligent network infrastructure that what the industry calls physical AI, autonomous machines actually operating in the real world, will ultimately depend on. It's a bigger ambition than simply making phone calls clearer or downloads faster; the argument is that the whole next wave of AI-powered hardware, from self-driving cars to factory robots, needs a wireless network smart enough to keep up with it in real time.
A Crowded, and Increasingly Geopolitical, Race

NVIDIA isn't approaching this alone or quietly. The company has built out an AI-RAN Alliance that now counts more than 130 participating companies, and has separately joined the US FutureG Office's OCUDU Initiative, a government-industry effort aimed at accelerating open, software-defined, AI-native 6G architecture domestically. NVIDIA has also put real money behind the bet, investing roughly $1 billion in Nokia as part of its broader push to use 6G as an entry point into the telecom hardware business it's historically had little presence in.

That flurry of alliances and investment isn't happening in a vacuum. Industry analysts tracking the space note that geopolitics has made the race toward 6G considerably more interesting than prior generational shifts, with multiple countries racing to shape the technical standards and supply chains that will define the next era of global wireless infrastructure. For the US specifically, backing an AI-native approach to 6G is being framed by some in the industry as a chance to reclaim ground in wireless leadership that shifted overseas during earlier network generations.
Still Early, and Not Everyone's Convinced Yet

For all the momentum, plenty of skepticism remains about how fast, and how completely, this vision actually gets built. Formal 3GPP standards work covering dedicated 6G studies isn't expected to wrap up until the 2026-2028 window, with commercial specifications not fully codified until closer to 2030 or 2031. Even within the industry, there's genuine debate about just how far AI hardware should physically extend into network infrastructure. A Samsung networks executive has noted that operators are still carefully weighing the total cost of actually putting GPUs inside base stations against the business case for doing so, a sign that the economics here are far from settled even as the technical vision gets more concrete.

Market forecasters, meanwhile, are penciling in a long runway before this translates into real revenue. Global technology intelligence firm ABI Research projects total 6G radio revenue will grow from roughly $8.1 billion in 2029 to $67 billion by 2034, with AI-chipset radio revenue specifically climbing from $1.8 billion to nearly $58 billion over that same stretch. Researchers at the firm describe 2029 through 2031 as the critical proving period, when operators will find out whether enterprise demand and AI-driven services can actually justify the scale of investment being discussed today.

us.headline: A One-Week Social Media Break Improved Young Adults' Mental Health
us.dek: Participants who quit TikTok, Instagram, X, Snapchat, and Facebook for seven days saw anxiety drop 16% and depression fall nearly 25%, per new JAMA research.
us.heroCaption: A young adult sets aside their phone, part of a week-long social media detox studied by researchers.

body.text: It turns out a week away from the scroll can do more for your mood than most people expect. A national study published in JAMA Network Open found that young adults who quit social media entirely for one week saw meaningful, measurable improvements in their mental health, with anxiety symptoms dropping by roughly 16%, depression symptoms falling by nearly 25%, and insomnia easing by close to 15%.

Researchers followed 373 participants between the ages of 18 and 24, first tracking a baseline week of ordinary social media use before inviting them into a week-long detox. Of that group, 295 opted in and agreed to stop using TikTok, X, Instagram, Snapchat, and Facebook entirely for seven days, giving the research team a genuinely apples-to-apples comparison of the same people's mental health before and after cutting the apps out.
The Twist: It Didn't Actually Reduce Screen Time

Here's the part that surprised even the researchers. During the detox, participants did cut their social media use dramatically, from just under two hours a day down to roughly 30 minutes. But their overall phone use barely budged, and in some cases even ticked up slightly, as people simply redirected their attention to other apps and activities instead of putting the phone down altogether.

That finding complicates a lot of the simpler advice floating around about digital wellbeing. It suggests the mental health benefit wasn't really about screen time in some general sense, phone use overall stayed roughly flat, but something more specific to what social media apps themselves do to people's mood and headspace when they're actively in the feed.
It's Not About How Much You Use It — It's How

Digging deeper into the data, the researchers found that objective usage metrics, like how many times someone opened an app or picked up their phone, didn't reliably predict who struggled with mental health and who didn't. What did predict it was something harder to measure from the outside: whether someone reported patterns of what researchers call problematic use, things like compulsively checking notifications, comparing themselves to others they see online, or feeling like they can't stop scrolling even when they want to.

Participants who reported those compulsive or comparison-driven usage patterns were considerably more likely to experience poor mental health than participants who used social media just as often but in a more passive, low-stakes way. Loneliness, notably, didn't change much for either group during the detox week, suggesting the apps' effect on mood operates somewhat separately from whatever role they play in helping people feel socially connected.
What This Means If You're Not Ready to Fully Quit

The findings arrive at a moment when concern about social media's effect on young people's mental health has become one of the more consistent themes in American public health conversation, with Johns Hopkins researchers and others regularly examining the science behind social media use disorder and its links to anxiety and depression in children, teens, and adults alike. This particular study adds a useful, practical data point to that broader conversation: even a short, temporary break seems to move the needle, without requiring someone to permanently delete their accounts or give up their phone.

For anyone weighing whether a digital detox is worth trying, the takeaway from this research is less about the total hours spent on a screen and more about noticing your own relationship to the apps themselves. If checking in feels compulsive rather than intentional, or if scrolling tends to leave you comparing your life to everyone else's highlight reel, this study suggests that's the pattern worth interrupting, even briefly, rather than screen time in the abstract.

us.headline: American Cancer Society Adds Colorectal Cancer Test Options
us.dek: The 2026 guideline adds a blood test alongside colonoscopy and stool-based options, aiming to reach the 20 million unscreened Americans as cases rise in adults under 50.
us.heroCaption: A patient discusses colorectal cancer screening options with a physician, following the American Cancer Society's updated 2026 guidelines.

body.text: The American Cancer Society updated its colorectal cancer screening guidelines this year with a straightforward goal: give more people an option that actually fits their life, so fewer people skip screening altogether. The 2026 update reaffirms that average-risk adults should start screening at age 45 and continue through 75, but it's the new menu of testing options that marks the real shift, adding a blood-based test taken during a routine doctor's visit alongside an updated and a brand-new at-home stool test.

Colonoscopy remains the gold standard in the guideline, both detecting and removing precancerous polyps in the same procedure. But the American Cancer Society has been explicit that expanding the list of alternatives isn't about replacing colonoscopy, it's about meeting the roughly 20 million eligible Americans, about one in three adults, who haven't been screened as recommended somewhere closer to where they already are.
Why the Stakes Keep Rising

The urgency behind this update isn't abstract. Recent American Cancer Society research found that colorectal cancer has become the leading cause of cancer death among adults under age 50 in the United States, a shift that would have seemed unthinkable a generation ago, when the disease was overwhelmingly associated with older adults. Robert Smith, the organization's senior vice president for early cancer detection science and senior author of the guideline update, said broadening the available screening tools is meant to help close that gap and catch more cancers while they're still at an early, treatable stage.

The numbers on early detection make the case for screening hard to argue with: five-year survival rates top 90% when colorectal cancer is caught early, a figure that drops sharply the longer a diagnosis is delayed. That gap between what early screening can achieve and how many eligible adults actually get tested is exactly the problem the new guideline is trying to close.
What's New on the Testing Menu

The headline addition is a blood-based test, marketed under the name Shield, which requires only a blood draw at a doctor's office and is recommended every three years for people who choose it over more invasive options. It joins two at-home stool-based tests, one updated version of an existing option and one entirely new addition, both of which work by detecting hidden blood or molecular markers that can signal the presence of polyps or early-stage cancer.

It's worth being clear-eyed about where these new options fit in the hierarchy, though. Visual exams like colonoscopy and stool-based tests remain the preferred screening methods in the guideline; the newer blood-based tests are included as a recommended option but not yet a preferred one, reflecting that they're a genuinely useful entry point for people who would otherwise skip screening entirely, even if they don't yet match colonoscopy's combined ability to both detect and immediately remove precancerous growths.
The Broader Screening Picture for 2026

Colorectal cancer isn't the only area where US screening guidance has shifted this year. Guidance for people ages 76 to 85 now explicitly frames continued colorectal screening as a personal decision, weighed against life expectancy, overall health, and prior screening history, rather than a blanket recommendation, while people over 85 are generally advised to stop screening altogether. Similar age-based, risk-adjusted frameworks now guide current US recommendations for breast, lung, cervical, and prostate cancer screening as well, part of a broader trend across American public health guidance toward more individualized rather than one-size-fits-all recommendations.

For anyone unsure where they fall in the current guidance, cancer specialists are consistent on one point: the specific test matters far less than actually getting screened. Whichever option someone is most likely to actually complete, whether that's a colonoscopy, an at-home stool kit, or a simple blood draw, is the right one for them, and talking through the options with a primary care provider remains the most reliable way to figure out which path fits an individual's risk factors and life circumstances.

us.headline: FDA Approves First-Ever mRNA Flu Vaccine After Refusing It
us.dek: Moderna's mFLUSIVA cleared regulators after an unusual reversal, arriving for the 2026-2027 flu season, with trial data showing stronger protection than traditional shots.
us.heroCaption: A vial of mFLUSIVA, Moderna's newly FDA-approved mRNA flu vaccine, set for release ahead of the 2026-2027 respiratory virus season.

body.text: The FDA just approved something it had refused to even look at a few months earlier. On August 5, regulators cleared mFLUSIVA, Moderna's messenger RNA flu vaccine, making it the first mRNA-based flu shot ever approved in the United States. The approval covers adults ages 50 to 64 outright, while adults 65 and older receive it under an accelerated approval pathway, one that allows broad use now but requires a follow-up study to confirm the full benefit down the line.

What makes this approval genuinely unusual isn't the science, it's the road it took to get there. Earlier this year, the FDA declined to even review Moderna's application at all, a rare move against a large pharmaceutical company that had run a substantial, largely favorable clinical trial. The agency only relented after real pushback from the pharmaceutical industry and public health experts, eventually convening a meeting of independent outside advisers in June before ultimately clearing the vaccine two months later.
Why the Fight Over This Vaccine Got Political

The FDA's initial refusal to review the application didn't happen in a vacuum. It came amid a broader climate of hostility toward mRNA technology within the current administration, with Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime vaccine critic, repeatedly condemning mRNA vaccines publicly. The administration has also cut funding for mRNA vaccine research more broadly and scaled back access to COVID vaccines during the same stretch, part of a wider backlash against pandemic-era vaccine mandates that spilled over into skepticism of the underlying technology itself.

Against that backdrop, the eventual approval reads as a genuine reversal rather than a routine regulatory milestone. Moderna CEO Stéphane Bancel framed it as proof of the continued strength and versatility of the company's mRNA platform, calling it an important new option for older Americans navigating a persistent public health challenge.
What the Data Actually Shows

Company research covering more than 40,000 participants found mFLUSIVA to be safe and, notably, associated with stronger protection than traditional flu vaccines, according to trial results shared with regulators. That protection matters given how severe recent flu seasons have been: the 2024-2025 season alone was linked to an estimated 45,000 deaths in the US, with flu-related hospitalizations and outpatient visits reaching their highest levels in fifteen years, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Experts are careful to frame mFLUSIVA as an additional option rather than a wholesale replacement for existing flu vaccines. Dr. Georges Benjamin, chief executive of the American Public Health Association, pointed to a different advantage entirely: mRNA vaccines don't rely on the decades-old process of growing vaccine virus in chicken eggs, a method that limits how quickly manufacturers can respond when a flu strain shifts unexpectedly. He said the technology could eventually let public health officials adjust to emerging flu strains far faster than the current system allows.
A Faster Path Ahead, If the System Adapts

Moderna has floated an even bigger long-term implication: the speed of mRNA vaccine production could eventually end the practice of selecting a single flu strain for an entire hemisphere each season, a system that's been the global norm for decades. In theory, individual countries could instead pick whichever strain match works best for their own population in real time, rather than committing to one forecasted strain many months in advance across an entire hemisphere.

For now, mFLUSIVA is expected to be available within weeks, in time for the 2026-2027 respiratory virus season. Whether the vaccine's arrival marks a genuine turning point for mRNA technology in the US, or simply one approval within a still-contentious regulatory and political environment, will likely depend on how the accelerated approval for older adults holds up once the required follow-up data comes in.

us.headline: US Hospitals Bet on AI as Doctor Shortage Grows Harder to Ignore
us.dek: With up to 86,000 physicians projected missing by 2036, roughly 80% of US hospitals now use AI clinically, though some doctors dispute the shortage itself.
us.heroCaption: A physician reviews AI-assisted documentation on a tablet between patient visits at a US hospital.

body.text: American hospitals are leaning on artificial intelligence harder than ever, and the numbers behind that shift are becoming hard to ignore. Roughly 80% of US hospitals now use AI in at least one clinical or operational function, according to industry data, and the Food and Drug Administration had cleared or approved about 1,250 AI- or machine-learning-enabled medical devices as of last year, a figure that keeps climbing month over month.

The pressure driving that adoption is demographic as much as technological. More than 10,000 Americans turn 65 and age into Medicare every single day, even as a wave of practicing physicians nears retirement themselves. The Association of American Medical Colleges projects the country could face a shortage of up to 86,000 physicians by 2036, an improvement from earlier, grimmer forecasts of 124,000, but still a substantial gap in a system where hospitals are already operating on razor-thin margins of roughly 1.5%.
Where AI Is Actually Making a Dent

The clearest, most measurable wins so far aren't in diagnosis, they're in paperwork. AI scribes and ambient listening tools, which automatically transcribe and summarize patient visits, are associated with a 40% to 45% reduction in physician documentation time, according to industry surveys. That matters more than it might sound: physicians have historically spent less than a third of their working hours actually with patients, with the rest swallowed by charting, notes, and administrative overhead that AI tools are increasingly absorbing instead.

A 2026 survey from Doximity found that adoption is already broadest among younger physicians, with more than 61% of doctors under 30 reporting they currently use AI in their practice, compared with 55% among physicians in their 50s. Neurology, gastroenterology, and internal medicine reported the highest current usage rates among medical specialties. Notably, even among physicians 60 and older, where adoption is lower, only 11% said they had no interest in using AI tools at all, suggesting resistance to the technology is fading even among more veteran doctors.
What Physicians Say They'd Do With the Time Back

The same survey asked doctors what they'd actually do with hours reclaimed from administrative work, and the answers cut against any narrative that physicians are simply looking to work less. Nearly 37% said they'd want to spend more time with their existing patients, while almost one in five said they'd use the freed-up capacity to take on new patients entirely, a detail that matters given how directly patient access ties back to the physician shortage discussion in the first place.
A Dissenting View: Is This Even the Right Problem?

Not every physician is convinced AI is solving the problem most people think it's solving. Dr. Marc Ayoub, a practicing physician, has argued publicly that framing this as a doctor shortage at all is a mistake, describing it instead as a distribution problem: the physicians largely exist, he argues, but the system is remarkably effective at preventing qualified doctors from practicing where patients actually need them, whether that's rural communities, specific specialties, or underserved regions. Under that view, pouring AI into hospitals that are already well-staffed does little to fix the deeper structural mismatch between where doctors are and where patients live.

That critique doesn't dismiss AI's usefulness so much as complicate the story around it. Even AI's more enthusiastic backers in the field tend to agree it won't fix reimbursement policy or single-handedly erase workforce gaps with a software update; the more grounded claim is that it can give physicians back meaningful hours in their day and reduce the burnout that's been pushing experienced doctors toward early retirement or reduced hours in the first place.
Diagnosis Is a Harder Problem Than Paperwork

It's worth being precise about where AI's clinical strengths actually sit right now. Narrow AI models, tools built for a single, well-defined task like flagging a particular pattern on a radiology scan, can already reach genuinely high, specialist-level performance. Radiology is where the vast majority of FDA-cleared AI medical devices are concentrated for exactly that reason. But more general-purpose AI systems, the kind that would need to weigh a complex, ambiguous case the way a physician does, still lag meaningfully behind human specialists on open-ended diagnostic reasoning.

That gap helps explain why most hospital AI deployments today are framed around triage, documentation, and flagging cases for physician review, rather than autonomous diagnosis. The technology's near-term role looks less like replacing physicians and more like clearing enough of the noise around them that the doctors who do exist can spend more of their limited time on the patients who need them most.

us.headline: Army Secretary Dan Driscoll Resigns Amid Hegseth Tension
us.dek: Driscoll's departure, effective September 3, follows a strained relationship with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the firing of top generals and Army readiness concerns.
us.heroCaption: Secretary of the Army Dan Driscoll testifies before Congress earlier this year, months before submitting his resignation.

body.text: Dan Driscoll's tenure as the Army's top civilian leader is coming to an end, less than two years after it began. The 26th secretary of the Army submitted his resignation to President Trump on Monday, according to multiple people familiar with the matter, with a departure date set for September 3. The move ends a run that started with real momentum and closed amid mounting tension with one of the administration's most powerful national security officials.

One source told reporters the decision wasn't a surprise given the friction between Driscoll and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. A second source said Driscoll's resignation letter raised concerns about the administration's approach to Army transformation and military readiness, and specifically pointed to Hegseth's role in blocking those efforts by removing the generals responsible for carrying them out.
A Relationship That Frayed Over Firings

The rupture between the two men traces back at least in part to earlier this year, when Hegseth fired Army Chief of Staff General Randy George along with two other senior generals. Driscoll had worked closely with George, and in April congressional testimony, he spoke warmly of the general's four decades of service and Purple Heart, calling him an amazing, transformational leader. Lawmakers from both parties pressed Hegseth on the firings at the time and voiced their own admiration for George, a sign the tension wasn't confined to internal Pentagon politics.

The strain reportedly deepened in the weeks before Driscoll's resignation. The Wall Street Journal, which first reported the departure, noted that Driscoll had already moved his family out of the formal Army Secretary's residence and into more modest housing by late August, a detail that outside observers read as an early sign he expected his time in the role to end soon. Other outlets had reported he was weighing a resignation around the Labor Day holiday.
Who Driscoll Is, and How He Got the Job

Driscoll, an Army veteran who served one deployment in Iraq and holds a Ranger tab, came to the role from a background in venture capital and Republican politics rather than a traditional military career track. He ran an unsuccessful 2020 campaign for North Carolina's 11th Congressional District before working as an advisor on Trump's 2024 reelection campaign, and is a close, longtime friend of Vice President JD Vance. He took over as Army secretary in February 2025 and simultaneously served as acting director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives until April of this year.

During his time in the role, Driscoll pushed hard on modernization and acquisition reform, and the White House credited him with helping negotiate elements of the Russia-Ukraine talks alongside his Pentagon duties. In a statement following the resignation, White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said Driscoll had been highly effective in advancing the administration's national security agenda and had provided outstanding leadership during a stretch of historic military operations.
What Happens Next

It's not yet clear who will step into the role. Under normal succession, the Army's undersecretary, a position currently held by Michael Obadal, would typically take over, and an Army official has described Obadal as having a strong working relationship with Hegseth. But Hegseth retains the authority to name whoever he wants to serve in an acting capacity, with no obligation to elevate Obadal either temporarily or as a permanent nominee.

One name already circulating as a possible successor is Sean Parnell, an Army veteran and political operative currently serving as the Pentagon's chief spokesman, who reporting earlier this year indicated had expressed interest in the job following the abrupt removal of General George. Driscoll's exit adds to a pattern that's defined Hegseth's tenure at the Pentagon since he took office in January 2025, one marked by a string of firings and early departures among senior military and civilian leadership.

us.headline: US Student Debt Nears $1.9 Trillion Amid New Repayment Rules
us.dek: Incoming freshmen are projected to graduate owing $43,000 on average, as new Tiered Standard and Repayment Assistance plans arrive alongside resumed wage garnishment.
us.source: Federal Reserve / CNBC / Department of Education
us.heroCaption: A college graduate walks across campus, part of a generation now carrying record levels of student loan debt.

body.text: The number keeps climbing, and it's climbing toward a milestone that would have seemed unthinkable a generation ago. Student loan debt in the United States approached $1.9 trillion in the first quarter of 2026, according to Federal Reserve data, up 3.1% from a year earlier and now spread across roughly 42.8 million Americans holding federal loans alone. For a country where higher education costs more, and is subsidized less, than in almost any other wealthy nation, that trajectory has become one of the more closely watched threads running through the broader US economy.

The rise isn't a mystery. Tuition has climbed roughly 5.6% a year on average over recent decades, consistently outpacing both inflation and household income growth, according to J.P. Morgan Asset Management. A growing number of schools have crept toward the $100,000 threshold for total annual cost of attendance, per data from The Princeton Review, and incoming college freshmen this year are projected to graduate owing an average of $43,000 in federal and private loans combined, according to a NerdWallet analysis released this spring.
Collections Resume, and Borrowers Are Feeling It

For borrowers already behind on payments, 2026 has brought real consequences rather than more warnings. The Trump administration resumed collections on defaulted federal loans back in May 2025, reinstating tools like wage garnishment and the seizure of tax refunds that had been paused for years during the pandemic-era relief period. As of the end of last year, $111.3 billion in direct loans sat in some stage of delinquency, affecting about 4.1 million borrowers and accounting for 18% of the direct loan repayment balance, according to Department of Education figures.

The scale of financial distress among borrowers extends beyond formal delinquency, too. Roughly 15% of people with a student loan payment due in a recent month either didn't pay at all or paid less than what was required, per the Federal Reserve's most recent Survey of Household Economics and Decisionmaking. Among borrowers already struggling, nearly a quarter had their loans handed over to a debt collector within the past year, a sign of how quickly financial trouble can escalate once a borrower falls behind.
A New Repayment System Arrives

Against that backdrop, the federal government rolled out a genuinely significant overhaul of how student loans get repaid. As of July 1, 2026, key provisions of what the administration calls the Working Families Tax Cuts Act took effect, replacing the tangle of previous repayment options with two simplified paths: a new Tiered Standard plan and an income-driven option called the Repayment Assistance Plan, or RAP. The Department of Education has framed the change as an answer to what it describes as a confusing maze of prior repayment structures that too often left borrowers owing more despite making consistent payments.

The rule went through a formal public comment period before taking effect, drawing more than 80,000 responses after being proposed in January. Most provisions kicked in this July, though some elements tied to loan rehabilitation, deferment, and forbearance won't take effect until 2027, and older repayment plans are set to sunset entirely by mid-2028, giving borrowers currently enrolled in those plans a runway to transition rather than an abrupt cutoff.
Are Colleges Actually Getting Cheaper?

The Department of Education has pointed to early signs that some institutions are responding to the new policy environment by trimming costs directly. The University of California, Irvine, for instance, cut tuition for its MBA program by more than 20%, a move the department has cited as evidence the broader legislation is nudging schools toward affordability. Whether that kind of price-cutting becomes widespread across higher education, or remains a handful of standout examples cited in a fact sheet, is a question that will likely take another admissions cycle or two to answer with any confidence.
A Generation Rethinking Whether College Is Worth It

All of this is unfolding alongside a broader shift in how American families are weighing the decision to enroll at all. Around 46% of this year's high school graduates are expected to go on to a four-year college or university, according to NerdWallet, a meaningful share but one reflecting a cultural conversation that's grown considerably more skeptical of college's return on investment than it was a decade ago. Research from Georgetown's Center on Education and the Workforce found that a full quarter of bachelor's degree graduates never fully recoup the cost of their education when measured against what they would have earned without the debt, a statistic that's been widely cited as colleges, students, and policymakers all try to figure out where the true breakeven point for a degree actually sits.

That skepticism is already reshaping enrollment patterns. While total college enrollment ticked up slightly to about 19.4 million students in fall 2025, driven largely by 3% growth at community colleges, private nonprofit institutions have seen enrollment decline even as the overall numbers hold roughly steady, with several smaller, tuition-dependent schools closing their doors entirely this year. For prospective students weighing their options, financial advisors increasingly frame the question less as whether to attend college at all, and more as which path, four-year degree, community college, trade program, or apprenticeship, offers the most sustainable debt-to-earnings outlook for their specific field.

sports.headline: Inside the NFL's AI System Mapping Players to Predict Injuries
sports.dek: The Digital Athlete program, built with Amazon Web Services, has helped drive a 25% drop in lower-extremity injuries since 2024, ahead of the 2026 season kickoff.
sports.heroCaption: Sensors and camera arrays track player movement during an NFL practice, part of the league's Digital Athlete AI safety program.

body.text: Football in 2026 runs on more than playbooks and film sessions. As the NFL kicks off its 107th season this month, the league's biggest technological bet is a program most fans have never heard of: the Digital Athlete, a joint venture with Amazon Web Services that treats player safety less like sideline medicine and more like a computational engineering problem, built to spot injury risk before it actually happens.

The scale of the data collection behind it is hard to overstate. Every player on the field gets mapped across 29 distinct body points, tracked 60 times per second, capturing joint alignment, torque, and asymmetry in enough detail to catch subtle biomechanical changes that would be invisible to a coach watching from the sideline or even reviewing film afterward. Across the league, the system processes roughly 500 million data points every single week, drawn from 38 high-resolution stadium cameras and sensors embedded in players' shoulder pads.
From Treating Injuries to Forecasting Them

The fundamental shift the program represents is philosophical as much as technical. Historically, football medicine has been reactive by necessity: a player gets hurt, and the medical staff responds. Digital Athlete flips that model, using AI simulations to model how force accumulates in a player's body over the course of a game or season, essentially forecasting structural stress before it turns into torn ligaments or fractured bone. League officials describe it as running a virtual biomechanics laboratory for all 32 teams simultaneously, rather than 32 separate medical staffs each working with whatever data their own franchise happens to collect.

That predictive capability now runs on serious computing muscle. The system has simulated more than 10,000 virtual football seasons to train its models, and it's built to deliver injury-risk inferences in under 100 milliseconds, fast enough to be useful in something close to real time rather than only in post-game analysis.
The Results Are Already Showing Up in the Injury Numbers

What makes this more than an impressive tech demo is that it's already shaping actual rule changes, and those rule changes appear to be working. Lower-extremity injuries have dropped by roughly 25% following two major interventions informed by the program's data: the 2024 Dynamic Kickoff rule redesign and the league's ban on hip-drop tackles. Both changes were built directly on patterns the Digital Athlete's models surfaced about where and how those specific injuries were actually occurring on the field, rather than relying purely on anecdotal coaching wisdom or historical injury reports.

That feedback loop, data revealing a risk pattern, the league adjusting a rule, and injury numbers actually improving afterward, is what NFL officials point to as validation that the investment is paying off in the metric that matters most to players and teams alike: games missed to injury. The league's broader Engineering Roadmap, a $60 million initiative managed through Football Research, Inc., has funded this kind of biomechanics work since 2017, when researchers first began simulating player impacts using modified crash-test dummies to understand how concussions actually happen on the field.
Part of a Bigger Wave Across American Sports

The NFL isn't alone in leaning this heavily on AI-driven biomechanics. San Francisco-based Infinite Athlete, formed through a 2023 merger of two established sports-tech firms, has built out its own player-tracking and biomechanics analytics platform used across multiple pro sports, reflecting how quickly this kind of technology has moved from research curiosity to standard infrastructure across American professional sports. A broader academic review published in 2025 found AI-driven biomechanics work concentrated heavily on two goals, improving athletic performance and predicting injury risk, with wearable sensors and motion-capture systems increasingly treated as standard training-room equipment rather than experimental add-ons.

For a league where player availability has become one of the most valuable and closely guarded competitive assets a team can have, that shift from reactive treatment to what officials call engineered availability management isn't just a safety story, it's increasingly a competitive one too. As the 2026 season gets underway, teams that can keep their best players healthy through data science, rather than luck or reduced practice intensity alone, are betting that translates directly into wins.

sports.headline: Carlos Alcaraz Returns From Injury to Open US Open Title Defense
sports.dek: The defending champion looked sharp in his first match back from a four-month wrist injury, as the US Open kicks off with a record $101 million prize pool.
sports.heroCaption: Carlos Alcaraz serves during his opening-round match at the 2026 US Open in Flushing Meadows, New York.

body.text: Carlos Alcaraz picked up right where he left off, which is exactly what a defending champion coming off a four-month layoff needs to do. The Spaniard opened his 2026 US Open title defense with a straight-sets win over Roman Safiullin, 6-4, 6-4, 6-4, looking sharp enough on his forehand and fit enough on his feet that any lingering concerns about his wrist injury faded almost as soon as the match got underway.

Alcaraz hadn't played competitive tennis in four months heading into Flushing Meadows, and while his serve wasn't hitting its usual top speeds, the rest of his game more than compensated. He saved five of six break points he faced and dominated at the net, winning 19 of 24 points when he came forward, the kind of aggressive, controlled performance that suggested the time off did little to dull his instincts on a hard court.
A Record-Setting Tournament Off the Court, Too

This year's US Open is making headlines beyond the results board as well. The tournament is offering a record $101 million total prize pool, the largest in tennis history and a 19% jump from last year's already-substantial $85 million. Running from August 23 through September 13 at the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center, the tournament closes out the Grand Slam calendar with both the men's and women's fields deeper and, thanks to the bigger purse, more financially lucrative than ever before for players across the entire draw, not just the eventual champions.
Other Big Names Made Their Mark Early

Alcaraz wasn't the only story of the tournament's opening days. Top-ranked Aryna Sabalenka cruised through her own first-round match, dropping just a handful of games against Camila Osorio, while American Ben Shelton needed four sets to get past Tallon Griekspoor in front of a home crowd clearly hoping for a deep run from one of the sport's rising domestic stars.

There was genuine upset drama too. Stefanos Tsitsipas, a former World No. 3 who's spent recent seasons trying to recapture his earlier form, pulled off his first top-10 win at a major since 2022, taking down Arthur Fils in four sets. Fils had entered the tournament fresh off a title run at the Cincinnati Open and was widely considered one of the players most likely to make a deep run in New York, which made Tsitsipas's win one of the tournament's more meaningful early results rather than just an opening-round formality.
American Players Have Reasons for Optimism

On the American side of the draw, ninth-seeded Taylor Fritz enters the tournament with real momentum, having won the Citi Open and reached the quarterfinals at the Cincinnati Open during this summer's hard-court swing, a stretch of form that positions him as one of the stronger domestic threats for a deep run. Taylor Townsend also delivered one of the tournament's notable early upsets on the women's side, knocking out 20th-seeded Maja Chwalinska, this year's French Open finalist, in straight sets.

With two full weeks of tennis still ahead before the women's final on September 12 and the men's final closing out the tournament on September 13, this year's US Open has already delivered the mix organizers hope for every year: a compelling comeback story at the top of the draw, genuine upsets shaking up the bracket, and enough depth in both American and international fields to keep the tournament's storylines shifting deep into the second week.

sports.headline: NFL Sets Record With Nine International Games, Eyes Future Team
sports.dek: Melbourne, Rio de Janeiro, and Paris join the NFL's global rotation for the first time, as Commissioner Roger Goodell confirms the league is eyeing an international franchise.
sports.source: NFL / Pro Football Hall of Fame
sports.heroCaption: Fans gather outside Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London ahead of an NFL International Series game, part of the league's record 2026 global slate.

body.text: The NFL isn't just testing the waters overseas anymore, it's diving in. The league has unveiled its most ambitious international slate yet for the 2026 season: nine regular-season games spread across four continents, seven countries, and eight stadiums, a new high-water mark in a global expansion push that's been building steadily for years.

Three cities are hosting NFL games for the very first time this season. The international slate kicks off in Melbourne, Australia, on September 10, when the San Francisco 49ers face the Los Angeles Rams at the Melbourne Cricket Ground, before the rotation extends to Rio de Janeiro and, for the first time ever, Paris, where the Pittsburgh Steelers and New Orleans Saints will play at the Stade de France on October 25. Established international markets aren't going anywhere either: London hosts three games this season, its 16th year in the rotation, while Madrid, Munich, and Mexico City round out the schedule.
A Milestone Nearly Two Decades in the Making

This year's expansion builds on a project that traces back to October 2005, when the Arizona Cardinals and San Francisco 49ers played the league's first regular-season game outside the United States at Estadio Azteca in Mexico City, a matchup that drew 103,467 fans and remains the largest crowd ever to watch an NFL regular-season game. That single game helped pave the way for the NFL International Series, which officially launched in 2007 and has since sent 62 regular-season games overseas, to markets including London, Berlin, Munich, Frankfurt, Madrid, Dublin, São Paulo, Mexico City, and Toronto.

NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell has framed the addition of Paris specifically as a genuinely significant next step in the league's global footprint, rather than simply another market checked off a list. Peter O'Reilly, the league's executive vice president overseeing international business, described this year's schedule as reflecting the NFL's global growth vision, bringing fans in new markets meaningfully closer to the sport rather than treating international games as one-off novelty events.
Beyond Single Games: A Real International Business Strategy

The single-game headlines are really just the visible surface of a much bigger commercial operation. The league's Global Markets Program, launched in 2022, grants individual NFL clubs marketing and fan-engagement rights in specific international territories, functioning as a longer-term investment in building fandom rather than a one-time event. All 32 teams now participate, with rights spread across 22 international markets, and the program added Italy as a new territory this year, with the Cleveland Browns and New Orleans Saints picking up marketing rights there while the Las Vegas Raiders expanded their own rights to cover Canada, the United Arab Emirates, and the United Kingdom.

That kind of structured, year-round international footprint, spanning broadcast deals, sponsorship, ticketing, and grassroots youth football development, marks a real shift from treating overseas games as neutral-site curiosities toward integrating them into the league's core commercial strategy on a permanent basis.
Could an International Team Actually Happen?

The bigger question hovering over all of this is whether the NFL eventually plants a full-time franchise overseas, and for the first time, league officials are talking about it as a real possibility rather than a hypothetical. Goodell has confirmed the league's intent to explore international expansion at the franchise level, and reporting suggests the league is weighing structures like an international division, potentially with four teams playing consecutive road games abroad to help manage the travel burden that's historically made an overseas franchise logistically difficult.

London has emerged as the clear frontrunner for that eventual team, given its two decades of hosting NFL games, an established and passionate local fanbase, and the practical advantage of no language barrier alongside direct flight access from major US cities. Germany, particularly Munich or Berlin, is considered the next-strongest contender, backed by a passionate following and a growing slate of annual games in the country. Whether any of this materializes into an actual franchise remains genuinely uncertain, but the league's tone around the question has shifted noticeably from deflection to active planning.

sports.headline: Teen Swimmers Rewrite the Record Books at 2026 US National Championships
sports.dek: Anna Moesch broke the American record in the 100m freestyle, while teen swimmers set new age-group marks in Irvine, alongside champions Caeleb Dressel and Kate Douglass.
sports.heroCaption: A swimmer competes in a freestyle final at the 2026 Toyota USA Swimming National Championships in Irvine, California.

body.text: The 2026 Toyota USA Swimming National Championships in Irvine, California, delivered exactly the kind of meet that keeps swim fans checking results in real time: a genuine mix of Olympic legends chasing new milestones and teenagers rewriting the record books right alongside them. Held over five days at the William Woollett Jr. Aquatics Center, the meet produced multiple American records and a wave of new national age-group marks, several of them set by swimmers still years away from their first Olympic Trials.

The standout individual performance of the meet belonged to Anna Moesch, who broke her own American record in the women's 100m freestyle, touching in 51.88 seconds to reset the national mark she'd already claimed. She backed that up the following night by winning the 200m freestyle in a personal-best 1:55.05, going out fast enough to sit nearly a full second ahead of the field at the midpoint of the race.
The Teenagers Weren't Just Along for the Ride

What made this year's meet particularly notable was how many of the headline moments came from swimmers barely old enough to drive. Liberty Clark claimed her third overall national age-group record of the meet in the 50m freestyle final, clocking 24.28 seconds, while a relay squad of Benjamin Jaggers, Max Laine, Sawyer Stolarczyk, and Julian Rusk set a new 15-18 age-group record in the 400m medley relay. In the women's 200m butterfly, an unnamed 17-year-old jumped into the national rankings by winning the title outright and setting a new 17-18 age-group record in the process.

Those performances reflect more than individual talent, they point to a genuinely deep pipeline of age-group swimmers pushing times that would have been unthinkable for their age category just a few years ago. Coaches and USA Swimming officials have pointed to improved regional training infrastructure and a broader, more competitive youth development system as key factors behind the surge in age-group records this season.
Sharing the Pool With Olympic Royalty

The rising talent competed alongside some of the sport's biggest names, which only raised the stakes further. Eight-time Olympic champion Caeleb Dressel, working his way through a comeback ahead of the Los Angeles 2028 Games, posted his fastest 100m freestyle time since the 2024 US Olympic Trials, touching in 47.70 seconds to claim the national title and signaling real progress in his return to top form.

Two-time Olympic champion Kate Douglass, fresh off breaking the 50m freestyle world record earlier in the year at the Pro Swim Series in Indianapolis, and fellow two-time Olympic champion Gretchen Walsh, who'd taken that same world record from Douglass just a week later, both headlined a women's 50m freestyle field that had fans buzzing well before the starting horn. Walsh went on to set a new American record of 24.51 in the event during the championship, adding yet another mark to what's already been a record-shattering year for the 50m sprint events.
What Comes Next

Notably, several of the country's top swimmers sat out Nationals entirely to focus their preparation on the 2026 Pan Pacific Championships in mid-August, meaning the meet's results represent only part of the full picture of American swimming's depth heading into the second half of the year. For the teenagers who did headline in Irvine, national team selectors say they'll be watching closely as those swimmers progress toward future international qualifying events, with several already being talked about as legitimate contenders for a spot on the senior national team well ahead of the traditional timeline.

sports.headline: US Marathon Demand Explodes, NYC Lottery Odds Hit Just 1%
sports.dek: More than 240,000 applied for roughly 55,000 New York City Marathon spots, while Chicago drew 200,000 applicants for 45,000 places this year.
sports.source: New York Road Runners / NBC News
sports.heroCaption: Runners fill the streets at the start of a major US marathon, as demand for entry spots reaches record levels nationwide.

body.text: Getting into a major American marathon has never been harder, and the numbers behind that statement keep getting more extreme by the year. New York Road Runners reported more than 240,000 applications for the 2026 TCS New York City Marathon drawing, chasing a field capped at roughly 55,000 runners, a gap that's pushed acceptance odds for non-guaranteed lottery applicants down to somewhere between 1% and 3%, worse odds than getting into an Ivy League college.

Chicago tells a nearly identical story. The Bank of America Chicago Marathon drew more than 200,000 applicants competing for roughly 45,000 to 50,000 spots in its 2026 race, and organizers say demand has kept climbing even as the field size has grown to accommodate more runners. It's not a one-city phenomenon, it's the new normal across the sport's biggest American races.
A Boom That Hasn't Slowed Down Since the Pandemic

The scale of this surge shows up clearly in the national participation data. According to RunSignup's RaceTrends report, overall US race participation grew 5% from 2024 to 2025, on top of 8% growth the year before that and 11% the year before that, a multi-year streak that's put to rest any lingering theory this was simply a temporary pandemic-era spike. Marathon finishers specifically jumped 14.6% in 2024 alone, and the 2025 TCS New York City Marathon set a world record as the largest marathon ever run, with 59,226 official finishers crossing the line.

Even Boston, which fills most of its field through qualifying times rather than a lottery, has felt the squeeze. For the 2026 race, the qualifying cutoff came in 4 minutes and 34 seconds faster than the previous year's standard, meaning runners who hit the official Boston Qualifying time on paper still weren't fast enough to actually get in. Race analysts describe that kind of compressing qualifying window as one more symptom of the same underlying pressure: too many runners chasing a supply of race bibs that simply can't expand as fast as demand.
Why the Physical Math Doesn't Work in Runners' Favor

Part of what makes this boom different from ordinary demand spikes is that the supply side genuinely can't stretch much further. City streets only hold so many runners at once, aid stations only cover so much ground, and most major marathons are already operating at or close to their physical capacity for a single-day event. London is exploring an expansion to a two-day race format targeting 100,000 total runners, one of the few majors actively experimenting with structural changes rather than simply tightening its lottery odds further.

That capacity ceiling has pushed race organizers, and runners themselves, toward workarounds. Charity entry programs have become one of the more reliable paths into sold-out majors: the 2025 Bank of America Chicago Marathon alone raised a record $47.1 million through charity runners, and roughly a third of this year's Chicago field is expected to be running on behalf of an official nonprofit partner, trading a hefty fundraising minimum for a guaranteed bib.
A Cultural Shift, Not Just a Sports Story

Much of this growth traces back to something bigger than the races themselves. Run clubs have exploded into genuine social hubs in cities across the country since the pandemic, turning what used to be a solitary training grind into a group activity built around community as much as competition. Strava's year-in-sport data has tracked a continued surge in new running club formation, and marathon culture more broadly has leaked well beyond its traditional endurance-sport niche, propelled by social media visibility, celebrity finishers, and a running shoe technology arms race that's made the marathon feel both faster and more achievable for everyday runners than it did a decade ago.

The performance data backs up that broader accessibility. The average American marathon finish time actually improved from 4 hours 39 minutes in 2019 to 4 hours 34 minutes in 2024, according to RunRepeat's analysis, even as the pool of participants running those times has grown dramatically wider and more varied. For runners still chasing a bib at one of the majors, race analysts increasingly offer the same practical advice: don't wait on the lottery alone, there are hundreds of other marathons across the country offering the same 26.2-mile achievement, often with a smaller field, a lower price tag, and just as memorable a finish line.

sports.headline: NBA Foundation Hits $165M in Grants for Grassroots Basketball
sports.dek: Six years after launching, the Foundation has served over a million under-resourced youth, while All-Star weekend in LA paired free hoops with facility renovations.
sports.heroCaption: Young players participate in a Jr. NBA basketball clinic, part of the league's expanding grassroots development efforts.

body.text: Six years into its existence, the NBA Foundation has quietly become one of the more substantial grassroots investment efforts in American professional sports. The organization marked its sixth anniversary this year having served more than 1 million under-resourced youth, built a portfolio of over 300 partner nonprofit organizations, and awarded $165 million in grants, crossing the halfway point of an initial $300 million commitment made when the Foundation launched in partnership with all 30 NBA teams back in 2020.

The Foundation's core focus has stayed consistent since its founding: workforce development and economic opportunity for under-resourced youth, with particular attention to organizations that are Black-controlled or deeply embedded in the communities they serve. Rather than simply writing checks, the Foundation asks applicant organizations to demonstrate measurable results, education outcomes, employment placement, or entrepreneurship growth among the young people they work with, before committing to what are often multi-year grant relationships.
All-Star Weekend Became a Community Investment Event

That grassroots emphasis was on full display when the league brought All-Star weekend to Los Angeles in February 2026. Beyond the on-court festivities, the NBA and its partners built five days of community-facing programming designed to reach more than 100,000 Los Angeles residents directly, an unusually large-scale commitment for a single event weekend.

The centerpiece was the Homecourt Hoops initiative, through which the LA Clippers distributed more than 5,600 free outdoor basketball hoops directly to families across the city. The Clippers have now refurbished more than 500 basketball courts across Southern California through their broader community efforts, addressing a genuine access gap: in the region, fewer than 35% of young kids play sports regularly, a decline of nearly 10 percentage points over the past decade, with almost 40% of families reporting they don't have a safe, walkable place nearby for their child to play at all.
Real Facilities, Not Just Symbolic Gestures

The All-Star programming went beyond distributing equipment. On February 12, the NBA, the National Basketball Players Association, the LA Clippers, State Farm, and the nonprofit Heart of America unveiled a full renovation of the Weingart YMCA Wellness & Aquatic Center, updating its STEAM lab, teen center, and basketball court as part of a broader legacy project timed to coincide with the YMCA's 175th anniversary in the United States. More than 1,000 local youth also participated in Jr. NBA and Jr. WNBA clinics that weekend, including sessions built around a curriculum developed through the Luka Dončić Foundation.

The league paired its youth programming with an economic development angle as well. The NBA Foundation hosted a pitch competition featuring seven Los Angeles-based entrepreneurs competing for $200,000 in total prize money, judged by celebrity panelists and backed by corporate partners including Comcast NBCUniversal, KKR, and American Express, an attempt to extend the Foundation's economic mobility mission beyond youth sports and into small business development in the same communities.
A Pattern That Extends Well Beyond One Weekend

This kind of investment isn't confined to marquee events. Individual players have built their own grassroots efforts alongside league-wide programming; Miami Heat center Bam Adebayo, a finalist for this year's NBA Social Justice Champion award, invested more than $563,000 through his own foundation into 18 separate initiatives this season, funding school supplies, transportation for thousands of students, and youth development programs including his own basketball camp across South Florida and North Carolina.

Nationally, the USA Basketball Foundation has been running its own parallel push, expanding youth development clinics with an explicit focus on reaching kids in diverse and underserved communities across the country, part of a broader landscape of NBA-affiliated and independent organizations, including the Jr. NBA Program and various team foundations, all working the same basic thesis: that widening access to coaching, facilities, and mentorship at the grassroots level is what ultimately builds a deeper, more diverse talent pipeline feeding the sport for the next generation.
